# Method

In this chapter the approach of this study is described. To answer the
research question, we performed an experiment to record data. A human
is sitting in front of a plant watching a video consisting of a lot of
short video clips to stimulate different emotions. The plant's voltage
signals and the human's HRV data are recorded as well as CO~2~ data. The
human's face is filmed during the experiment, which is used to label its
emotion. This is used as input for the training of the machine learning
models. CO~2~ is also recorded in order to search for correlations as a
basis for future research.

## Architecture Overview

The system is organized as a sequential data pipeline that transforms
raw multimodal sensor recordings into a trained plant-based emotion
classifier, complemented by a separate real-time inference component, a
live dashboard. @fig-pipeline provides an overview. The pipeline consists
of five stages — sensing, preprocessing, labeling, modeling, and live
application — each described in turn below. The CO~2~ correlation
analysis branches off the same recorded data as a separate confound test
rather than forming a stage of its own.

![Overview of the system pipeline. Colour marks the role each stream plays: green is the plant signal, the only family the classifiers ever see; blue is the human reference from which the proxy labels are derived; purple is the environmental variable used for the confound test. Dashed arrows denote evaluation and downstream use rather than data flow.](figures/pipeline.png){#fig-pipeline width=100%}

**Sensing.** Four independent sensors capture the raw data: plant
electrodes record the plant bioelectric voltage at a nominal 100 Hz, a
webcam records facial expressions, a Polar H10 chest strap records heart rate
and R-R intervals, and an SCD41 sensor records ambient CO~2~. Because the
Polar H10 yields both heart rate and HRV, these four sensors produce five
distinct data streams. The sensor setup builds on the implementation by
Gloor [@gloor2025].

**Preprocessing.** Each session consists of one participant watching a
sequence of short emotion-eliciting video clips while the five streams
are recorded. The sensors run independently; their readings are aligned
into one shared event log only after recording, together with the
corresponding video file. This common time base is then divided into
non-overlapping 30-second windows, which form the unit of analysis for
every stage that follows.

**Labeling.** The windows are turned into a proxy emotion label. Valence
is derived from facial expression via HSEmotion and arousal from HRV; the
two are crossed into a five-class emotion label.

**Modeling.** The plant voltage of each window is reduced to a set of
statistical, spectral, and signal-dynamics features, and the labeled
windows of all sessions are merged into a single consolidated dataset.
Three classifiers — Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network — are then
trained and compared separately for emotion, arousal, and valence, using
plant-bioelectric features only, and the best model per axis is selected
by macro-averaged F1.

**Live application.** The selected models are reused in the live
dashboard, which infers emotion in real time; because the offline
normalization requires an entire session's data, the dashboard instead
normalizes each window only against the windows preceding it.

Alongside these stages, the CO~2~ correlation analysis tests whether
ambient CO~2~, rather than the person, could account for whatever
association the classifiers establish. It therefore addresses H2 and
contributes nothing to the classifier itself.

The complete implementation of every stage described in this chapter —
firmware, recording, labeling, dataset creation, the three model
pipelines, the correlation analysis, and the live dashboard — is publicly
available in the project repository [@repo2026]; @sec-appendix-code maps
each stage to the file that implements it.

## Sensor Setup

The sensing stage relies on four independent sensors: plant electrodes,
a camera, the Polar H10, and the SCD41 CO~2~ sensor. This section
describes the hardware behind each of them, starting with the plant
sensing setup itself.

The plant sensing hardware builds on the ESP32 and AD8232 architecture
previously used for plant biosensing by Gloor's group [@gloor2025]. The
AD8232, originally designed as a heart-rate front end, is repurposed
here to amplify the weak bioelectric signal of the plant. The ESP32
microcontroller samples the amplified signal at 380 Hz internally,
decimates it, and streams the result over WebSocket at a configured
output rate of 100 Hz. Because the decimation factor is an integer, the
rate actually delivered is higher than the configured one: measured
against the recording timestamps it is approximately 119 samples per
second. Every rate-dependent feature is therefore computed against the
rate measured for that session rather than the nominal one, and the
pipeline refuses to window a session whose measured rate departs from the
expected value by more than ten percent.
Only this hardware front end was adopted; the recording,
synchronization, labeling, and machine-learning pipeline were developed
independently for this project.

A single *Kalanchoe* plant was used throughout all recording sessions.
Three standard medical electrodes, of the same type used for ECG
recordings, were attached using their adhesive surface to the three
largest leaves of the plant. Each electrode was connected to the AD8232
board, which forwarded the resulting voltage signal to the ESP32 for
transmission.

In addition to the plant voltage, the ESP32 also measures an SCD41
sensor, which reports ambient CO~2~ concentration in ppm. CO~2~ is not
sampled at a fixed rate but logged once per received data batch. Two
further sensors complete the setup: a Polar H10 chest strap, connected
via Bluetooth Low Energy, providing R-R intervals for the later
HRV-based arousal label, and a standard webcam recording the
participant's face for the FER-based valence label.

The entire sensor setup was assembled and operated in the Digital Lab of
the Cologne Institute for Information Systems.

## Field Work

Recording is orchestrated by the recording component. None of the four
sensors acts as a master clock; instead, each sensor writes its readings
independently into one shared event log, timestamping every entry
against the local system clock of the recording computer. This design
avoids the need for a common hardware trigger, at the cost of requiring
the four streams to be aligned after the fact rather than during
acquisition. The output of a completed session is this shared event log
together with the
corresponding video recording, which together form the raw input to
every following processing step.

Participants were recruited from fellow students, personal
acquaintances, and other students unknown to the team beforehand. All
participants were between 20 and 30 years old and from Germany. In
total, 15 participants completed one session each.

The emotional stimulus consisted of a video of approximately ten minutes
in length, reused from an earlier COIN seminar project [@schafer2025].
The video follows a fixed sequence of emotionally contrasting segments,
beginning with light-hearted content such as clips of dogs and a
humorous advertisement, and later introducing material intended to evoke
disgust, shock, and sadness, including scenes of a more graphic and
violent nature. It ends with an extended unsettling sequence that
concludes with a jump scare. All participants viewed the clips in the
same fixed order.

During the session, participants were seated at a table facing the
laptop and asked to watch the video without any additional task.
Participants were informed verbally about the nature of the video,
including the possibility of disturbing or graphic content, and were
asked whether there were any topics they did not want to be confronted
with. Each participant completed the session alone in the room, and the
room was ventilated between sessions.

The participant sat at the table directly in front of the laptop running
the video and the recording code. The plant with the attached electrodes
stood on the table to the left of the laptop, well within the
participant's field of view, and the breadboard carrying the AD8232 and
the ESP32 sat in front of the plant, connected to it by the electrode
leads. @fig-setup in @sec-appendix-figures documents this arrangement.

## Labeling Algorithm {#sec-labeling-algorithm}

Self-assessment ratings, for instance following the Self-Assessment
Manikin [@bradleylang1994], would provide a direct subjective report
("honest signal") for each window. They were deliberately not used here,
because such ratings may be influenced by conscious or unconscious
response bias and therefore do not serve as an independent ground truth.
Instead, valence and arousal are derived from separate physiological and
behavioral channels, processed independently, and combined in a final
step to form the crossed emotion label.

Before these channels can be processed, the independently timestamped
sensor streams must first be brought onto a common time grid. Each session is divided into 30-second windows based
on elapsed recording time, and every sensor reading is assigned to the
window whose interval contains its timestamp; only once the plant
voltage, facial video, and R-R interval series have been aligned in this
way can values from different sensors within the same window be treated
as referring to the same moment in the session. This window length
follows Baek et al. [@baek2015], who show that 30 seconds is the shortest interval
from which HRV metrics can still reliably approximate the much longer
five-minute windows recommended by standard HRV guidelines. These
30-second windows are non-overlapping and form the grid used for
calibration and model training; a denser, overlapping 5-second grid is
additionally computed only for the inspection plots shown later in this
chapter and plays no role in calibration or training.

Before any HRV measure is computed, the raw R-R interval series recorded
by the Polar H10 is corrected for artifacts using the beat
classification method of Lipponen and Tarvainen [@lipponen2019],
implemented in NeuroKit2 [@makowski2021]. A single misdetected heartbeat
can otherwise distort every downstream HRV value, so correction is
applied per window before the arousal signal is derived.

Valence is derived from facial expressions. Video frames are sampled at
5 Hz and each sampled frame is passed through HSEmotion
[@savchenko2022], a model trained on the AffectNet corpus
[@mollahosseini2019] that outputs a continuous valence estimate per
detected face. These per-frame estimates are averaged per window,
weighted by the model's own confidence, to obtain a single valence value
for that window (@eq-fer-valence). Windows in which a face was detected
in too small a share of the sampled frames are excluded rather than
labeled (@eq-coverage).

Arousal is derived from HRV by combining RMSSD with mean heart rate into
a single index. Both quantities are computed per window from the
corrected R-R series (@eq-rmssd, @eq-hr). Since RMSSD decreases with
physiological activation while heart rate increases with it
[@kreibig2010], RMSSD is inverted before the two measures are averaged.
Both quantities enter this index as robust z-scores relative to the
session's own median and spread (@eq-robust-z), yielding the single
arousal index of @eq-arousal.

Because resting heart rate, HRV, and facial expression differ
substantially between individuals, no single threshold could separate an
emotionally salient window from a neutral one across all participants: a
resting heart rate of 90 bpm might indicate heightened activation for
one person and be entirely unremarkable for another. The labeling
algorithm therefore has no fixed notion of "normal"; instead, each
session's own data is used to establish what counts as this
participant's baseline on that day, against which deviations are then
judged.

Both axes are then discretized using the same logic, independently
applied and centered on the participant's own session median. A window
is classified as positive or negative in valence, or as activated or
calm in arousal, when its value lies outside a deadband of half-width
$\tau$ around that median; otherwise it falls into the respective
neutral category (@eq-valence-class and @eq-arousal-class). The deadband
is sized from the spread of the session's own values, as given in
@eq-tau. Median and MAD are recomputed independently for each session,
from that session's own non-overlapping 30-second windows introduced
above, so that a participant's individual resting level and spread
define the reference against which their own windows are judged. The
multiplier $k$ in @eq-tau, by contrast, is fixed at 0.5 for both axes,
setting the half-width of the neutral deadband to about half a robust
standard deviation around the median. This value was chosen once, before
the main analysis, by inspecting a pilot session, so that a substantial
share of windows still received a directional (non-neutral) label rather
than collapsing into the neutral category; it was deliberately not
re-estimated per participant, keeping the labeling rule identical across
all sessions. The two resulting labels are then crossed into the final
emotion label (@eq-crossing), following the logic of the circumplex
model presented by Russell [@russell1980] and shown in
@fig-circumplex: if either the valence or the arousal label is neutral, the
window is assigned the overall label *neutral*; only if both axes are
non-neutral is the window assigned one of the four directional labels,
*negative activated*, *negative calm*, *positive activated*, or
*positive calm*, formed by combining the non-neutral valence category
(negative/positive) with the non-neutral arousal category
(calm/activated). This crossing rule follows directly from the quadrant
structure of the circumplex model [@russell1980], in which only the four
outer quadrants correspond to a clearly directional affective state,
while any window touching the neutral zone on either axis is treated as
affectively unspecific.

## Feature Engineering

For every 30-second window, a set of features is extracted from the
plant voltage signal alone. These fall into three families: (i)
time-domain amplitude and shape descriptors (mean, median, standard
deviation, detrended standard deviation, interquartile range, range,
root-mean-square, zero-crossing rate); (ii) spectral descriptors from a
Welch power spectrum (band powers in four frequency bands, their ratios,
and spectral entropy); and (iii) signal-dynamics descriptors (Hjorth
activity, mobility, and complexity, and a spike rate counting transient
excursions beyond three robust standard deviations from the median). This
yields 22 feature columns per window; @tbl-features lists them
individually with their definitions, together with the six quality
columns that accompany them into the design matrix.

Each feature is provided in two representations that are compared during
training: *raw*, the value on its original absolute scale, and
*session-normalized*, a per-session robust z-score obtained by subtracting the
session median and dividing by the scaled median absolute deviation
computed over that session's own non-overlapping windows
(@eq-snorm). The session-normalized representation removes
between-session offsets in the plant signal that are unrelated to the
participant's emotional state.

To assemble the training data, the labeling pipeline is run over every
recorded session, producing one file of non-overlapping labeled windows
per session (one row per window). The presence of a labeled file is
verified for each session; all files are then loaded, checked for an
identical column schema, and concatenated into one consolidated dataset.
Duplicate windows (identified by session and window start time) are
removed, and windows the labeling pipeline could not classify (label
"excluded") are dropped. The final dataset therefore contains only
successfully labeled, non-duplicate windows.

## Machine Learning Models

The classifier predicts the arousal, valence, and emotion label of each
30-second window from the plant-bioelectric features only. For a given
target, the other label axis, the crossed emotion label, and all HRV-
and FER-derived columns are excluded from the features, so the model
sees nothing derived from heart rate or facial expression — the plant
signal is the sole predictor family. The classes are: arousal (calm,
neutral, activated), valence (negative, neutral, positive), and emotion
(negative calm, negative activated, neutral, positive calm, positive
activated).

Before training, rows without a target label are removed, remaining
missing feature values are imputed with the column median, constant
(non-informative) features are dropped, and the target is label-encoded.
Three classifiers are then trained and compared, each on both feature
representations (raw and session-normalized), giving six combinations per
target:

- **Random Forest** with balanced class weights;
- **XGBoost**;
- **Neural Network** (multilayer perceptron) wrapped in a
  StandardScaler pipeline, since, unlike the tree-based models, it is not
  scale-invariant.

These three names are used throughout the paper. The comparison figures in
@sec-results are generated by the pipeline itself and therefore label the
same models with their code identifiers `RandomForest`, `XGBoost`, and
`NeuralNet`, and the two representations as `raw` and `session_norm`.

Because the classes are imbalanced — a large neutral class dominates
each target — overall accuracy would largely reflect the majority class.
Macro-averaged F1, which weights every class equally, is therefore used
as the primary selection and comparison metric, complemented by
accuracy, one-vs-rest ROC-AUC, a confusion matrix, and a per-class
classification report.

Models are evaluated with a nested, participant-grouped, stratified
k-fold cross-validation:

- windows are **grouped by participant**, so that no participant appears
  in both the training and test portion of a fold, preventing
  participant-level leakage;
- folds are **stratified** by class to keep class proportions comparable
  across folds;
- the **outer** loop (5 folds) provides the held-out test estimate,
  while an **inner** loop (3 folds) performs hyperparameter tuning by
  grid search on each outer fold's training data only, so the test folds
  never influence tuning.

For each target, the (model, representation) combination with the
highest macro-F1 is selected as the winner and used in the live
dashboard, and its significance is assessed with a label-permutation test
over 200 shuffles of the target. Re-running the nested search inside every
permutation is computationally out of reach, so the test instead holds the
winning architecture fixed at its full-dataset-tuned hyperparameters and
refits only that, once on the real labels and once per shuffle, across the
same participant-grouped folds. The observed statistic the null
distribution is compared against is recomputed the same way, so the two
are commensurable and the resulting p-value is calibrated against its own
null rather than against the nested estimate. A separate tuning on the
full dataset supplies those fixed hyperparameters, the feature-importance
rankings, and the model persisted for the live dashboard.

## Live Demonstration {#sec-live-demonstration}

To demonstrate the whole setup, we developed a single dashboard that
shows every data source at once. This includes the live signals detected
by the sensors: plant bioelectric voltage, CO~2~, heart rate, and camera
feed. In addition, two values per axis (arousal, valence, emotion) are
calculated and displayed side by side. On the one hand, it shows the
proxy labels, applied live to HRV and FER using the same labeling rule.
On the other hand, it presents the corresponding plant-model predictions
of arousal, valence, and emotion. These predictions originate from the
pre-trained models; for each axis, the model with the best macro-F1
score is applied to every 30-second window.

Placing the two values per axis directly next to each other makes the
comparison between the plant model and the labeling algorithm the visual
centre of the display. @fig-live-dashboard in @sec-appendix-figures shows
the dashboard during a session, captured in a window in which the two
agree on positive valence but disagree on arousal — the qualitative
pattern that the quantitative results in @sec-results reproduce.

Every live signal updates continuously. Only the two predictions per
axis are window-based. Both recompute once every window of data has been
collected. There is no training here; the winning models are only loaded
once. To teach what is "normal" for the participant in the particular
session (e.g. heart rate), the labeling algorithm performs a one-time
calibration based on the entire recorded session and knowing all
windows. However, the live dashboard has no fixed session end to
batch over, which is why the calibration is recomputed after each
completed window. Therefore, it is growing across the live session and
updates in real time. After each new window, the median and MAD are
recalculated based on all previous windows, and the longer the session
runs, the more stable and accurate the "normal value" becomes. At the
beginning of a session, the classification is therefore less reliable
than later on.

The same pipeline was also operated in a reduced configuration for
demonstration purposes, independently of the recording sessions; this is
the state the photograph in @fig-setup was taken in. Two differences to
the recording configuration are deliberate. First, the CO~2~
sensor is omitted: CO~2~ is recorded only as a candidate confounder for
the correlation analysis and enters none of the trained models, so
dropping it removes hardware without affecting inference. Second, the
screen runs a German-language variant of the dashboard, built for the
Phaenomena exhibition, at which a comparable live plant-emotion
demonstration was shown in 2025. It reduces the
panel layout of @fig-live-dashboard to the single comparison that carries
the project's message — what the camera-based FER recognizes ("Das
erkennt die KI") next to what the plant model infers ("Das spürt die
Pflanze") — above one live voltage trace and a confidence bar. The plant,
electrodes, AD8232, and ESP32 are unchanged, so the signal path feeding
the models is identical to the one used during recording.

## Correlation Analysis

The correlation analysis is the study's secondary test. It examines H2,
the possibility that ambient CO~2~ rather than the person accounts for
the association established under H1, and it is carried out on valence,
because valence is the dimension for which that association holds; on an
axis where no effect is found there is nothing for a confounder to
explain.

The confounding structure under test is the following. When a
participant's emotional state changes, their breathing changes, which in
turn alters the CO~2~ concentration in the room, and that concentration
may affect the voltage measured between plant and electrode. CO~2~ is
thus associated with both sides of the plant–valence comparison, and were
that shared dependence the whole story, the plant would appear to track
valence without responding to the person at all.

We therefore test the three pairwise relationships forming this triangle
(plant–valence, plant–CO~2~, CO~2~–valence) and use the partial Spearman
correlation $\rho(\text{plant}, \text{valence} \mid \text{CO}_2)$ as the
decisive test. It is computed across all 22 plant features
(@tbl-features) in two complementary variants: a raw analysis (variance
both between and within sessions) and a session-normalized analysis
(variance within-session only). Two conditions must hold together for
H2 to survive: both branches of the CO~2~ pathway must be present, and
controlling for CO~2~ must collapse the plant–valence correlation toward
zero. If either branch is absent, or if the correlation persists once
CO~2~ is controlled for, CO~2~ cannot account for the plant–valence
relationship and H2 is rejected.
